content: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are infections transmitted through sexual contact, including vaginal, oral, and anal intercourse. Examples of STIs include chlamydia, syphilis, trichomoniasis, gonorrhea, herpes simplex virus (HSV), human papillomavirus (HPV), hepatitis B, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Globally, STIs affect millions of individuals, particularly those aged 15 to 24 years, as well as older populations. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), there are approximately 357 million new cases of four major STIs annually: chlamydia (131 million), gonorrhea (78 million), syphilis (5.6 million), and trichomoniasis (143 million). Additionally, over 290 million women are affected by HPV infections, one of the most common STIs. In the United States alone, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reports 20 million new STI cases annually, with an estimated lifetime healthcare cost of $16 billion. STIs can lead to significant health complications. For instance, gonorrhea and chlamydia can cause prostatitis and pelvic pain in men, while women may experience pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility. Syphilis is associated with stillbirths, congenital malformations, and neonatal mortality. HPV is a known cause of cancers in the cervix, vulva, vagina, penis, anus, and throat. Many STIs are asymptomatic or go unrecognized, which means that individuals who do not regularly access healthcare services may miss timely diagnosis and treatment. This is particularly concerning for young people, who often do not seek care for STI symptoms, leading to a higher burden of disease among women of reproductive age. The problem is exacerbated in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), where STIs are more prevalent, and access to healthcare is limited. Given the widespread use of mobile phones and social media among young people, particularly in LMICs, Short Message Service (SMS) has emerged as a potential tool for delivering information and strategies to prevent high-risk sexual behaviors and STIs. Digital media technology (DMT), which includes text, audio, video, and graphics, can be used for health education and promotion. Mobile technology, especially SMS, offers a cost-effective, accessible, and convenient method for delivering health interventions. Unlike face-to-face sessions, SMS-based interventions can overcome barriers such as transportation and infrastructure limitations, allowing individuals to seek care without revealing their identity or facing the stigma associated with in-person consultations. Mobile phone text messaging (MPTM) involves sending brief electronic messages between devices over a phone network. SMS is widely used globally, with approximately 3.8 billion mobile phone users in developing countries as of 2011. Mobile phones are owned by 67% of the world’s population, making SMS a promising tool for STI prevention. SMS is inexpensive, instantly accessible, and available on nearly all mobile phone models. It is also asynchronous, meaning messages can be accessed at a time convenient for the recipient. This feature is particularly useful in resource-poor settings where access to advanced technology is limited. SMS also supports interactivity, allowing users to seek additional help when needed. For example, motivational messages, behavior-change tools, and interactive components such as Quit Buddy programs can be adapted for delivery via SMS. Text messaging has been shown to be effective in promoting behavior change by delivering tailored health communication. Messages can be designed based on theoretical models such as the theory of planned behavior and the health belief model. SMS has been used in clinical settings to improve knowledge about STIs, increase retesting rates, and encourage healthier sexual behaviors. For example, one study found that the annual rate of chlamydia testing among young people increased from 7% to 12% after SMS-based health messages were implemented. Increasing chlamydia testing rates is crucial for reducing the duration and transmission of the infection. Text messages can include information about STI testing, treatment, prevention, and motivation for retesting. Examples of messages include: Chlamydia: hard to spell, easy to catch. Use a condom, Chlamydia can cause infertility, and Most STIs have no symptoms; the only way to know is to get tested. SMS can also serve as a reminder for clinical appointments, such as You are due for your next screening. In sexual health services, SMS is commonly used for appointment reminders, rescreening, delivering test results, promoting sexual health, and assisting with contact tracing. Studies have shown that SMS interventions can reduce the time from diagnosis to treatment, increase retesting rates among high-risk groups, and decrease missed clinic appointments. By improving knowledge, understanding, and self-efficacy, SMS technology can encourage individuals to adopt healthier behaviors, such as avoiding risky sexual practices, thereby reducing STI incidence rates. Periodic prompts and reminders via SMS have been found to be effective in reinforcing healthy behaviors and improving communication. Repeated messages can increase the likelihood of positive behavioral changes. SMS is particularly beneficial for individuals who may feel embarrassed or stigmatized by in-person consultations. In such cases, telephone-based interventions can provide a more comfortable alternative. Additionally, SMS is a cost-effective and measurable method for delivering healthcare interventions, even in resource-limited settings. However, the effectiveness of SMS for STI prevention may be limited by factors such as illiteracy and the character limit of text messages. Adolescents and young adults under the age of 24 have the highest incidence rates of STIs, with a disproportionate number of new infections occurring in this age group. The rising incidence of STIs highlights the urgent need for innovative prevention strategies. Despite the potential benefits of SMS for STI prevention, the evidence remains inconclusive due to the small sample sizes of existing studies. To date, no comprehensive review has been conducted to evaluate the impact of text messaging on STI prevention. Further research is needed to determine the effectiveness of this intervention.
